one_liner: CPython 3.8 fork plus pip-installable JIT module (DynASM baseline JIT, quickening, inline caches); about 10-30% faster than stock CPython 3.8.
what_it_does: Pyston ships in two forms. Pyston-full is a complete CPython 3.8.12 interpreter with a JIT and other interpreter and build changes, distributed as deb, portable, conda and Docker builds; it is source (API) compatible, but every C extension must be recompiled for it. Pyston-lite is a C extension module for stock CPython 3.7-3.10 that replaces the eval loop with the JIT; `pip install pyston_lite_autoload` turns it on at startup and keeps existing binary wheels working.
how_it_is_fast: A very cheap baseline JIT (Python/aot_ceval_jit.c) uses LuaJIT's DynASM to emit machine code straight from bytecode, with no IR. That removes dispatch overhead, and a 'deferred value stack' skips value-stack pushes and pops and some refcount updates. Hot opcodes call ahead-of-time generated, type-specialised C traces (e.g. float*float), and the JIT adds inline caches for attribute and global lookups. A code object is JIT-compiled after about 200 calls or generator resumptions (JIT_MIN_RUNS = 2 x OPCACHE_MIN_RUNS). Pyston-full adds quickening, other CPython optimisations, and an LTO+PGO+BOLT, non-PIE build; pyston-lite is itself built with PGO, LTO and BOLT.
when_to_use: Long-running web services (Django, Flask style) pinned to CPython 3.8 that cannot move to a newer CPython yet
You want a JIT without rebuilding any C extensions: pyston-lite wheels exist for CPython 3.7-3.10 on Linux x86-64/aarch64 and macOS x86-64/arm64
Interpreter-bound pure-Python code heavy on attribute access, global lookups and Python-level calls, which the inline caches and the dispatch removal target
A drop-in change to throughput on a CPython 3.8 fleet is worth more than PyPy's larger gains, because PyPy means changing implementations
when_not_to_use: You are on CPython 3.11 or newer: nothing supports it (issue #298 about 3.11 support for pyston-lite has no reply), and newer CPython releases already include much of this work

Anything that needs ongoing security or bug fixes: the project is declared no longer maintained, with the last code change in Feb 2023 and open crash reports (#299 GC crash, #307/#296/#295 recursion crashes, #310 _curses)
pyston-lite on aarch64 servers: issue #305 reports SIGSEGVs on AWS Graviton with gevent, PyYAML and kafka-python, with no fix
Windows (no builds or wheels), musl/Alpine (no musllinux wheels, #279), or systems that forbid writable+executable memory
Workloads that spend their time inside C extensions (NumPy, regex, I/O): the JIT only speeds up Python bytecode execution

integration.form: module (pyston-lite wheel for CPython 3.7-3.10) or full interpreter binary (pyston-full: deb, portable directory, conda, Docker image pyston/pyston)
integration.dependencies: none at runtime. Building from source needs clang, LuaJIT (DynASM preprocessing), and LLVM and BOLT submodules, with LLVM built twice for the PGO build
integration.min_toolchain: Building needs GCC with the global-register-variable extension (aot_ceval_jit_helper.c, compiled without LTO), -std=gnu99, clang and luajit; lite builds need Python 3.7-3.10 headers. Pyston-full runs Python 3.8.12 code.
integration.platforms: JIT supports only x86-64 (System V ABI) and AArch64; Linux x86-64/aarch64 for pyston-full; pyston-lite wheels for Linux x86-64/aarch64 (manylinux2014) and macOS x86-64/arm64 (no cp37 arm64); BOLT step only on x86 Linux; no Windows
integration.thread_safety: Same GIL model as CPython 3.8; JIT thread-safety beyond that is not documented
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — pyston-lite runs on stock CPython 3.7-3.10 and keeps binary wheels working; pyston-full is API- but not ABI-compatible with CPython 3.8, so every C extension must be recompiled (no prebuilt packages per the README)

gotchas: On Linux the JIT maps its code chunks PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE|PROT_EXEC (MAP_32BIT on x86-64; MAP_JIT only on macOS), so it needs writable+executable memory. It silently stops compiling once 100 MB of JIT code is used (JIT_MAX_MEM env var). Setting JIT_PERF_MAP runs system("rm -rf /tmp/perf_map").

Harness flaw in the repo's own `make bench` (pyston/tools/benchmarks_runner): the baseline is whatever distro python3.8 is installed, not the same source built with the same flags. The printed geomean covers only flaskblogging and djangocms. In those benchmarks the requests client and the server both run on the interpreter under test. analyze.py's per-benchmark ratio divides the system build's all-iterations mean (warmup included) by a post-warmup mean for the other builds, a small bias toward the JIT builds; the geomean line uses post-warmup means for both.

The project wiki's 'pyperformance on windows10' page compares native Windows CPython 3.8.10 with Pyston 2.3 inside WSL2 Ubuntu, i.e. two different operating systems. Its outliers (pathlib 10.19x, startup 4.13x) reflect the OS difference, not the JIT.

Code can tell which variant is active with hasattr(sys, 'pyston_version_info') (full) or 'pyston_lite' in sys.modules (lite). CPython tracing support works by deoptimizing back to the interpreter, so profilers and debuggers run without the JIT's speedup.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Pyston only if you are stuck on CPython 3.7-3.10 and need a speedup without changing implementation or code. PyPy gives much larger gains on long-running pure-Python loops but is a separate runtime. Cython, mypyc and Codon require compiling or annotating your code. The CPython tail-calling interpreter needs Python 3.14 and gives 3-5%, but it is maintained.
verified_claims_summary: The README claims Pyston-full is 'roughly 30%' faster than CPython on web-serving macrobenchmarks and pyston-lite 'roughly 10%' (the lite PyPI text says 10-25%); no CPU, compiler, run count or CPython build is given. The in-repo harness behind such numbers runs flaskblogging, djangocms and kinto from pyston/python-macrobenchmarks against the distro python3.8 and reports post-warmup per-request means. A Pyston blog result known only from a search snippet (blog blocked here) reports +65% on pyperformance for Pyston-full 2.3.5 versus CPython 3.8 on an EC2 c6i.xlarge, against +26% for CPython 3.11rc2.
status_note: Declared no longer maintained (last code change Feb 2023, last pyston-lite release 2.3.5 on PyPI 2022-09-26) and frozen at CPython 3.8.12 (full) and 3.7-3.10 (lite) with open crash reports. The PSF/Python-2.0 licence makes it legally copyable, but it is a legacy option, not one to adopt for new deployments.
sources_read: WebSearch: 'Pyston 2.3 vs CPython 3.11 benchmark pyperformance comparison' (blog.pyston.org and phoronix.com snippets only)
